title: Unclipped Fall-Arrest Lanyard
whatIsWrong: A worker is wearing a full-body harness at height, but the fall-arrest lanyard hook is left dangling and unclipped from any anchor point.
whyItsSuspicious: A harness only protects a worker if it's actually connected to a rated anchor at all times when working at height. An unclipped lanyard offers zero protection if a fall occurs.

title: Damaged Ladder
whatIsWrong: A worker climbs a ladder with a visibly cracked and missing rung that was never inspected or tagged before use.
whyItsSuspicious: Every ladder needs a pre-use visual inspection and a current inspection tag. A damaged rung can give way mid-climb, and skipping the check removes the last line of defense before someone gets hurt.

title: Missing Guardrails
whatIsWrong: Guardrails are fitted on one side of the elevated platform, but a worker is standing right at the open, unprotected edge on the other side.
whyItsSuspicious: Guardrails are a collective protection measure — they only work if they surround every open edge. A partial installation creates a false sense of security while the real fall hazard remains exposed.

title: Overloaded Scaffold Platform
whatIsWrong: Stacked materials, drums, and two workers crowd a scaffold deck well past its posted safe working load, with no load-rating signage visible.
whyItsSuspicious: Scaffolds are engineered for a specific maximum load. Exceeding it risks structural failure or collapse — and without a visible load rating, crews have no way to self-check before adding more weight.

title: Unprotected Opening
whatIsWrong: An open deck hatch has no cover, barrier, or warning sign, and a distracted worker looking at a phone is walking straight toward it.
whyItsSuspicious: Uncovered openings need a physical barrier or cover plus clear signage regardless of how experienced the workforce is. Distraction plus an unguarded opening is exactly the combination that leads to a fall-through incident.

title: Improvised Anchor Point
whatIsWrong: A worker's lanyard is clipped to a process pipe running along the wall instead of the rated anchor point located nearby.
whyItsSuspicious: Only anchor points rated and certified for fall-arrest loads should ever be used. A pipe, handrail, or piece of equipment can fail under fall-arrest force even if it looks sturdy enough to lean on.

title: No Permit or Rescue Plan
whatIsWrong: The crew is already working at height, but the permit board shows no signed-off work-at-height permit and no rescue plan on file.
whyItsSuspicious: A permit-to-work forces a documented check of hazards and controls before work starts, and a rescue plan is what gets a fallen, suspended worker down safely within minutes. Starting without either removes both the pre-check and the safety net.

title: Working at Height in High Wind
whatIsWrong: Wind speed is visibly above the safe working limit — flags and equipment are blown near-horizontal — but work at height continues instead of being stopped.
whyItsSuspicious: Wind loading affects balance, swinging loads, and the stability of ladders and scaffolds. Crossing the site's wind-speed threshold should trigger an automatic stop-work and reassessment, not a judgment call to push on.
